speaker: John
line: Today's lecture is on R-S-I-Forge. In our graduate seminar on research agents, we keep returning to a practical question: how can we tell whether an agent has improved a research solution? Recent work such as Agent-as-a-Judge and Training A-I Scientists to Replicate Research reflects growing interest in evaluating agent work and reproducing science. R-S-I-Forge takes a related but distinct direction: it uses published papers to build runnable tasks and independent reference solutions. I see a hand—yes, Noah?

speaker: Noah
line: Hi, Professor. Is the central idea mainly to give agents more time to solve research problems?

speaker: John
line: Not quite. The paper starts from a bottleneck: evaluating research improvement requires both a challenging task and a trustworthy way to score solutions, and building those usually takes scarce expert and engineering effort. R-S-I-Forge divides that work among agents with separate responsibilities. Its collection contains 210 environments across 18 fields. The goal is to make repeated changes to solutions measurable, not to claim that the agents have advanced the original scientific research.

speaker: John
line: The pipeline begins with an author agent, which adapts a paper’s method and research question into a bounded task. It prepares a starting solution, data-generation code, an evaluator, and separate development and held-out test sets. A reviewer checks whether the instructions are usable and whether the evaluator measures the stated objective. When checks fail, the task can go back for repair; accepted tasks are not simply one-shot generations.

speaker: Noah
line: Quick question: what makes the reproduced method an independent baseline rather than just another starting solution?

speaker: John
line: A reproducer implements the paper’s method independently using solver-facing materials, without access to the author agent’s implementation or construction history. It also does not receive the test data or target score. Its implementation is evaluated on held-out data as a separate reference point. The starting solution scores 0, and a task-specific target defines 1; that target helps normalize scores but is not necessarily attainable. Of the accepted main-run environments, 79% needed at least one revision.

speaker: John
line: That distinction matters when interpreting the solver study. Four models each made 3 successive attempts on 120 environments from the main run. A new session inherited earlier code and notes, but began with a fresh context; the model weights stayed fixed. At least one model improved by 0.01 or more in normalized score after the first session in 84% of environments. At least one surpassed the reproduced baseline in 68 of 120.

speaker: Noah
line: So does beating that baseline mean the agent discovered a better scientific result?

speaker: John
line: No. These are gains on bounded tasks adapted from papers, not evidence of progress on the original research problems. The study measures changes to task solutions, not learning in model weights or general research ability. Also, 95% of sessions that beat the reproduced baseline were coded as involving work beyond parameter tuning. But that category includes repairs and evaluating alternatives, and the transcript labels were generated by a model without human validation; it cannot establish scientific novelty.

speaker: John
line: Human review adds another view of what these environments can and cannot measure. Experts rated room for improvement above a starting solution at 4.81 out of 5 and score discrimination at 4.74. The three-judge panel’s corresponding means were 4.89 and 4.65. But experts rated resistance to saturation lower, at 3.09, compared with the panel’s 3.98. Saturation asks whether one idea might exhaust a task; it is a distinct concern from whether scores separate stronger solutions.

speaker: Noah
line: Can we treat those rating gaps as evidence that the judges were too generous?

speaker: John
line: Not on their own. Experts reviewed 90 of the 180 main-run environments, one expert per environment, and did not receive exactly the same evidence as the agent judges. Experts also rated shortcut resistance and fidelity to the source paper more critically. These are judgments about rubric dimensions, not direct proof that every evaluator is valid. The comparison is useful as a diagnostic, while its differences in evidence and limited expert coverage need to stay visible.

speaker: John
line: The paper also compares ratings with R-S-I-Exam, which evaluates repeated improvement on executable research tasks. On different, unpaired task sets, the same three agent judges rated R-S-I-Forge higher for score discrimination and shortcut resistance, but lower for resistance to saturation. That contrast does not isolate the effect of automated construction. More broadly, the paper contributes a process for building and inspecting tasks; the result does not show that automation itself makes an environment better.

speaker: Noah
line: How should we read the example trajectory without overgeneralizing from it?

speaker: John
line: One example follows a Claude Opus 5 agent on a humanoid foothold-selection task. Its three final submissions rise from 0.15 to 0.33 to 0.58 in normalized held-out score. Across sessions, the agent changes how it searches candidate footholds and checks ground support. That illustrates what an inherited solution path can look like, but one trajectory cannot explain the aggregate gains or show which particular change caused them. Some held-out grading material was also accessible during solver runs.

speaker: John
line: The larger implication is a more concrete way to study agent work: construct bounded tasks from published methods, attach an independently reproduced reference, and observe how solutions change across attempts. This complements work focused on judging projects or reproducing papers, while asking a different evaluation question. Future studies can test how robust these environments are, whether their results transfer, and what causes improvement. This study does not establish that inherited records, rather than extra solving time, produced the gains.

speaker: John
line: The key takeaway is to separate a measurable improvement on an adapted task from progress in science or self-improvement in a model. R-S-I-Forge offers a multi-agent approach to constructing executable research tasks and comparing solutions against reproduced methods. Its results support using such environments to examine agent behavior, while also exposing questions about fidelity, shortcuts, and saturation. Thanks for listening. If you have any further questions, ask our A-I assistant or drop a comment.
